query: For multicomponent high-entropy alloys in solid and liquid states at and near their high melting temperatures, what single testable methodological intervention could overcome the inability of EAM references to represent the many atomic configurations of the ab initio liquid? Explain why it should improve reference–target phase-space overlap, predict the reduction in thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to TOR-TILD’s EAM references, define the applicable composition and temperature ranges, identify supporting evidence from elemental or binary calculations, and specify a decisive free-energy benchmark that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Replacing static EAM reference potentials with an actively‐learned machine‐learning interatomic potential (ML-IAP) that is trained on ab initio data from high-temperature disordered liquid and near-melting solid configurations will better capture the many-body, chemically complex environments in multicomponent high-entropy alloys. This improved potential will yield a reference that has enhanced phase-space overlap with the ab initio target phase, thereby reducing the thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to current TOR-TILD EAM references.
generation.material_initial_state: A multicomponent, refractory or transition-metal based high-entropy alloy (with 4–8 principal elements) in its disordered liquid state and high-temperature solid state (near 0.9–1.0 Tm).
generation.intervention: Develop and employ an on-the-fly, actively-trained ML interatomic potential (e.g., Moment Tensor Potential or neural network potential) that is continuously updated using ab initio molecular dynamics data from representative high-temperature configurations of the target HEA. Use this ML potential as the reference potential in thermodynamic integration (TOR-TILD) calculations.
generation.conditions: Applicable at temperatures at and near the high melting point (approximately 0.9–1.0 Tm) for multicomponent HEAs with significant chemical and configurational disorder; the approach is expected to be most effective for systems where EAM shows large configuration-to-configuration variability (e.g., systems with >4 elements and strong local chemical fluctuations).
generation.structural_mediator: The ML potential is designed to sample the full spectrum of atomic environments (including local short-range order in the disordered liquid and high-T solid states) that mediate free energy contributions, thereby bridging the structural gap between the reference and target phase spaces.
generation.mechanism: An ML-IAP trained on a broad set of ab initio configurations will adjust its energy landscape to account for the high variability in atomic environments (both in terms of bond angles and local chemical ordering) that EAM potentials oversimplify. This leads to enhanced overlap between the reference free energy surfaces and those of the true ab initio liquid. In turn, the integration path mismatch in free-energy calculations is reduced because the ML-IAP provides a more accurate interpolation over the many atomic configurations present at high temperature.
generation.predicted_outcome: The integration path mismatch in thermodynamic integration should be reduced substantially (potentially by on the order of 50% relative to TOR-TILD’s current EAM references) when using the ML-IAP. As a result, the computed free energies (e.g., liquid free energy) will converge closer to ab initio benchmarks within a tighter error margin.
generation.baseline: TOR-TILD thermodynamic integration calculations using static EAM reference potentials that are known to inadequately represent the extensive configurational diversity in the ab initio liquid.
generation.boundary: This method is expected to work primarily for systems with high configurational complexity (multicomponent HEAs) near high melting temperatures. It may be less beneficial (or require re‐training) for alloys with very low melting points or for systems that are already well described by EAM due to simpler bonding environments.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of reduction in the path mismatch is presently approximate, and the exact improvement will depend on the quality of the ML training set and the complexity of the alloy. Moreover, the computational cost of on-the-fly training and validation in multi-component systems is yet to be fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform thermodynamic integration for a representative multicomponent high-entropy alloy near its melting temperature by using two different reference potentials: (1) the standard TOR-TILD EAM reference and (2) the newly developed ML-IAP reference. Both integration paths should be computed over an identical series of ab initio snapshots. Compare the resulting free energies to those obtained from direct ab initio molecular dynamics integration.
measurements: Free energy per atom over the integration path
Thermodynamic integration error (mismatch) between reference and target phase-space
Deviation (in meV/atom) of computed free energies from a direct ab initio benchmark
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the ML-IAP-based integration does not reduce the thermodynamic-integration path mismatch by a significant margin (e.g., less than ~20% improvement) or if the free energies computed using the ML reference do not converge closer to those obtained from direct ab initio calculations (e.g., within an error margin better than ~20 meV/atom) when compared to the standard EAM-based TOR-TILD approach.

cited_evidence.text: Paper card. Question: How does chemical short-range order (SRO) affect the mobility mechanisms of screw and edge dislocations in the MoNbTaW refractory high-entropy alloy over a wide temperature range?. System: MoNbTaW refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA), specifically comparing a random solid solution (RSS) and an equilibrium state with SRO at 800 K. Processing: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations using a machine-learning moment tensor potential (MTP); SRO states were equilibrated using a hybrid MD/Monte Carlo (MD/MC) approach at 800 K; dislocation lines created with a periodic length of ~15 nm. Test conditions: Shear stresses ranging from 0 to 3.0 GPa applied at temperatures from 300 K to 2000 K. Findings: At 300 K, the presence of SRO provides an extra strengthening of approximately 180 MPa for screw dislocations.; The strengthening effect of SRO on screw dislocations attenuates with increasing temperature, becoming negligible at 2000 K where mobility curves for RSS and SRO samples overlap.; A cross-slip locking mechanism is observed for screw dislocations, where jogs form on different slip planes, causing the dislocation to become immobile or requiring extra stress to unlock.;
